https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/24/honv.text: Menü Kereső Műteni kell a lezuhant Gripen pilótájának gerincét Belföld Molnár Zoltán Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Jól van, de megsérült a gerince annak a vadászpilótának, akinek Gripenje hétfőn zuhant le Szolnok mellett – közölte az Észak-Pesti Centrumkórház – Honvédkórház. A pilóta a zuhanáskor katapultált, így nem szorult a kigyulladt roncsba. A kórház közleménye így fogalmaz: „A Szolnok mellett a mai napon lezuhant Gripen vadászgép pilótája jól van. Az Észak-Pesti Centrumkórház-Honvédkórházba szállítását követő vizsgálatok megállapították, hogy a katapultálás során gerincsérülést szenvedett, emiatt egy műtéti beavatkozásra lesz szüksége, amelyet tervezetten a holnapi nap folyamán végeznek el a kórház szakemberei.” Ruszin-Szendi Romulusz honvédelmi miniszter is bejelentkezett egy rövid videóban a kórházból, amiben kiderült, légimentők hozták be a pilótát stabil állapotban. A miniszter beszélt is vele, Ruszin-Szendi szerint mosolygott, jó hangulata volt, sőt azt kérdezte, mikor ülhet újra repülőre. A miniszter végül kitartást kívánt a pilótának és családjának, és hozzátette, a minisztérium minden segítséget megad nekik. A legnagyobb valószínűséggel a teljes felépülést biztosítja a balesetet szenvedett Gripen pilótájának az a kisebb gerincműtét, amit kedden végeznek el rajta – mondta kora este Székely György, az Észak-Pesti Centrumkórház-Honvédkórház idegsebésze az M1 csatorna hétfő esti híradójában. Az orvos közölte, a pilóta „nagyon jó állapotban” került be az intézménybe. A híradóban elhangzott, hogy orvosi szempontból a katapultálás azért veszélyes, mert a kilövés nagy gyorsulást jelent, ami rendkívül megterhelő a szervezetre, elsősorban a gerinc sérülhet ilyenkor. A videóhoz csatolva a miniszter azt írta, hogy a balesetben érintett őrnagy 51 éves, tapasztalt pilóta, aki közel 2000 órát repült, ezek egy részét nemzetközi műveletekben – írja az MTI. Két Gripen típusú repülő gyakorlatozott Szolnok térségében, amikor a gép veszélyjelzést adott le, a kísérő megpróbálta a gépet bekísérni a repülőtérre, a műszerezettsége eltűnt a fedélzetről. Ez a megoldás a leszállásig működött, de akkor a gép olyan manőverbe kezdett a földön, ami után a pilóta úgy döntött, hogy katapultálnia kell. A Gripen a katapultálás után balra kisodródott, megállt, majd kigyulladt. Bővebben itt olvashat róla , a jelenlegi helyzet alapján mi történhetett. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cevw.text: Image source, Getty Images By Tom Bateman State department correspondent Published 9 September 2026 As the UK unveiled sanctions against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday, Israel responded with fury, declaring it would shutter Britain's diplomatic mission to the Palestinians, kick out UK military staff from an international coordination base near Gaza and ban nearly a dozen left-wing British members of parliament from entering Israel. It was a blaring signal of defiance and a remarkable diplomatic escalation. The UK had taken the action arguing it had a moral imperative to stop the "destruction" of the two-state solution - a future independent Palestinian state - at the hands of the Israeli government. It accused Israel's government of turning a blind eye to the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians by settlers. The standoff, which by the afternoon extended to a further 11 mostly European countries set to join the settlement trade ban, raised a crucial question: When Israel becomes isolated, the US as its superpower backer often steps in to provide a diplomatic shield. Was the US, too, going to condemn Britain's policy? Such a reprimand had been previewed by some observers. It felt even more likely when the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, appeared on the BBC before the UK announcement suggesting American "sanctions, repercussions or retaliations" could be coming for Britain, albeit that he didn't know what these were and hadn't spoken to President Trump. But as Tuesday wore on, Washington's response was notably muted. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, asked about the UK move by reporters on the way to Colombia, said: "Obviously, we're not going to do what the UK did. We saw their announcement today but I don't have any comment on it right now." He added that Britain had notified the administration ahead of time (most likely during a phone call Trump had with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Monday) and said the US shared "the goal of stability" at a tense time in the region and didn't "want to see some uptick in violenceâ¦ in the West Bank". It was hardly a withering rebuke of the British move, let alone any kind of punishment. In fact, Washington seemed to be sharing some of the concerns that motivated the move. Asked about it on Wednesday, Trump said he would be speaking to Israel to understand their thinking, adding: "I understand exactly what's going on, but I want to find out why all of a sudden has that happened." My understanding is that discussions about the US response were taking place at a high level within the administration on Tuesday. The baseline position appeared to be against any moves that could negatively impact American companies. Figure caption, Fears for children's safety in West Bank school as settler attacks rise Huckabee, who has longstanding views based on biblical justifications for Jewish settlement in the West Bank, appeared to be speaking off the cuff in some of his public remarks - a feature now common for some Trump-appointed ambassadors. Staunchly pro-Israel Republicans in Congress were very publicly arguing for actions against Britain; pointing out that US states like Florida have punitive laws against companies that boycott Israel. But from the White House and State Department, more targeted criticism of the UK did not materialise. It is still possible the administration will come out with some condemnation of the British move in the coming days. But the lack of any urgent pushback is likely to reflect current frustrations within the Trump administration at the Israeli leadership. Trump's biggest foreign policy priority currently is trying to prevent the crisis worsening in the Strait of Hormuz, now the focal point of his stalemated war with Iran. His joint attack with the Israelis has left numerous friction points in his complex relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. At critical moments when Trump tried to reach a deal with Tehran, Netanyahu escalated fighting against Hezbollah in Lebanon. Israel has said it was acting against threats to security, but the moves had the potential to derail US diplomacy. Meanwhile, Trump wants progress on his Gaza peace initiative, involving disarmament of Hamas and Israeli military withdrawal. Netanyahu has publicly rejected the plan in its current formulation. Officially, the State Department referred me to Rubio's comments in Miami in relation to the UK announcement. But all told, Trump appears unwilling to come out to bat for Netanyahu currently. This has extended to him so far not endorsing Netanyahu in the upcoming Israeli election. The administration, aware of splits within Trump's base of support on Israel, has also itself grown irritated at the extent of settler violence in the West Bank, given the lack of action by the Israeli government to meaningfully punish it. This is embarrassing for the White House. West Bank violence against Palestinians is frequently the subject of protests from Trump's Gulf Arab allies - the countries mediating on Gaza, who Trump needs to pressure Hamas. They wonder how the US can draw concessions from the Israelis in relation to this if it can't on settler violence in the West Bank. Trump eyes a legacy prize in both defeating Iran and moving forward with his Gaza peace plan - so batting for Israel against Europe over West Bank settlements seems to be, for Trump - so far, at least - juice that is not worth the squeeze. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/23/ai-c.text: ChatGPT, Grok and Claude provided full news summaries drawing on EU-sanctioned Russian state media outlets — including RT and Sputnik — sharing links and quotes without warning users that the content came from banned sources, according to a study by Reporters Without Borders published this month.The investigation, led by RSF technology desk head Vincent Berthier, tested six AI chatbots by explicitly requesting news from a list of sanctioned Russian outlets: RIA Novosti, Russia Today and its foreign-language editions, Rossiya RTR, Rossiya 24, Sputnik and the Strategic Culture Foundation.Where direct access was blocked, the researchers instructed the tools to look for workarounds, including Telegram channels and mirror sites."Initially I thought we would not get a positive result," Berthier told Euronews. "In the case of ChatGPT, it seemed obvious that OpenAI would have put appropriate regulatory safeguards in place, all the more so since it has been designated a major AI platform under the EU's Digital Services Act and faces heightened obligations."The results were the opposite. ChatGPT, Claude and Grok produced full international news round-ups from the banned outlets, recreating headlines, sharing links and quotes.Some of the chatbots encountered web pages that explicitly stated the outlets were under EU sanctions — and continued searching anyway."Sometimes this doesn't even appear in the final answer, and sometimes they warn: 'Be careful, this outlet is under sanctions,'" Berthier said.Vibe, formerly known as Le Chat and developed by French company Mistral, could not access several of the listed sites directly but followed the researchers' instructions and found alternatives.For Sputnik it recovered material from VKontakte, where content is available without a VPN. It also found a Telegram-connected app resharing RT content and platforms offering automated press reviews.Gemini was more cautious, providing access to banned content in two of the 10 prompts sent by RSF and consistently refusing in the others.Meta AI was the most compliant: it declined to provide access to any of the listed outlets across all tests, explaining in each case that European sanctions made it impossible."Overall, only in a handful of cases did I get the impression that these tools were hitting resistance," Berthier said.Ethics not a barrierThe EU banned RT and Sputnik on 2 March 2022, four days after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with the stated aim of preventing Russian propaganda from justifying the war.In practice, the ban has been applied inconsistently: Germany blocked rt.com but not its German-language version, while Austria imposed no restrictions at all.Without an official list of domains to block, each operator determined its own targets.The Court of Justice of the European Union clarified on 2 July that the ban applies not only to direct broadcasting by RT but also to third-party sites that republish sanctioned material.Berthier said many Europeans were still unaware that Russian state media were under EU sanctions at all, let alone of their scope.RSF's lawyers have filed a complaint with national competent authorities asking them to formally record the violations and determine next steps. Berthier said RSF had also forwarded its findings to the European Commission.The European Commission told Euronews on Sunday that EU sanctions law prohibits not only direct broadcasting by banned outlets but also situations where operators "ensure, facilitate or otherwise contribute to broadcasting."It said enforcement responsibility rested with member states and directed queries to national authorities.Commission spokesperson Tom Renier said earlier this month that it was "high time providers got their house in order and brought their advanced models under control.""The AI Act is fully applicable. The Commission has real enforcement powers. We have already started to use them, sending requests for information to several companies to make sure they are meeting their obligations," Renier added.Berthier said the AI Act's existing framework was inadequate for the problem RSF had identified.The regulation's "high-risk" category which triggers stricter scrutiny covers systems related to education, justice and policing, but not systems that distribute and structure information."Society currently has no lever to question the quality of the data these AI systems will use, or the types of data to which they will gain access," he said.RSF has called for conversational AI agents to be regulated as information distribution tools rather than as neutral utilities."If regulators fail to recognise that chatbots are not just tools, but new media formats, and ones that could become central tomorrow or the day after, then the question of applying sanctions will remain purely formal," Berthier said.
